questions.q: What does DefaultAzureCredential() do when called with no arguments?
options: It automatically tries a real ordered list of credential sources — environment variables, Managed Identity, then a local sign-in — until one works
It immediately fails unless a password is passed in directly
It only works if the script is never run outside the Azure portal
It generates a brand-new service principal every time it runs
questions.explain: DefaultAzureCredential walks a real, ordered chain of credential sources automatically, with no secret passed into the call itself.

questions.q: In what order does DefaultAzureCredential typically check its sources?
options: Environment variables (service principal), then Managed Identity, then a local signed-in session like az login
It checks sources in a random order every time it runs
It only ever checks a hardcoded key inside the script
Managed Identity first, then it refuses all other sources
questions.explain: The chain checks environment variables for a service principal first, then Managed Identity on an Azure resource, then a local sign-in session.

questions.q: What does boto3.client("s3") check when called with no explicit key arguments?
options: Its own credential chain: environment variables, the ~/.aws/credentials file, and an IAM role attached to the compute resource
Nothing — it will always raise an error without an explicit key
Only a hardcoded key stored inside the boto3 package itself
It requires logging into the AWS web console first, every single run
questions.explain: Boto3 walks its own ordered credential chain, the same way DefaultAzureCredential does for Azure.

questions.q: Why does an IAM role attached to an EC2 instance matter for authentication?
options: It lets boto3 authenticate automatically with no access key to manage, type, or accidentally commit to source control
It replaces the need for the boto3 package entirely
It only works for S3 and no other AWS service
It requires the instance to be manually re-authenticated every hour
questions.explain: An IAM role attached to the compute resource is fetched automatically through the instance metadata service — no long-lived key required.

questions.q: Why do both credential chains avoid ever requiring a secret to be hardcoded in the script?
options: A hardcoded secret sits in the file (and source control history) forever, readable by anyone with access to the repo
Hardcoded secrets are technically impossible to write in Python syntax
Hardcoding a secret would make the script run faster
Cloud providers block scripts that contain any string literals
questions.explain: This ties directly to the broader security principle that a secret written into source code is effectively permanent and widely exposed.
